notes: Complete costs appeal judgment on whether success fees could be assessed on post-discontinuance summarily assessed costs.

enrichment.short_title: Success fees not recoverable on summarily assessed costs where proceedings had concluded under CPR 44.3A(2)(a)
key_facts: Thompson sued Anderson for defamation, discontinued, and was ordered to pay two thirds of her costs, partly summarily assessed by Master Rose and McCombe J.
Anderson's bill on detailed assessment included success fees under conditional fee agreements on those summarily assessed sums.
Costs Officer Emery allowed success fees totalling £3,900; Thompson appealed, contending the Masters had already made a summary assessment of all costs including additional liability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to a High Court costs judge against a costs officer's allowance of success fees on detailed assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; respondent ordered to pay appeal costs of £1,351.25.
enrichment.ratio: Once proceedings have concluded, CPR 44.3A(2) applies and a judge who summarily assesses costs without ordering detailed assessment of the additional liability is treated as exercising power under rule 44.3A(2)(a); a costs officer cannot go behind that order and separately allow success fees on summarily assessed costs.
legal_issues: Whether success fees on summarily assessed post-discontinuance costs were assessable on detailed assessment
Whether Master Rose and McCombe J made summary assessments under CPR 44.3A(2)(a), (b) or (c)
Whether failure to specify base costs and additional liability separately prevented summary assessment of success fees

notes: Complete Chancery appeal judgment on partnership vicarious liability and causation in accountant share fraud claim.

enrichment.short_title: Accountancy firm partners liable for senior partner's forged share transfers as acts in ordinary course of business
key_facts: Senior partner Gordon forged stock transfer forms to sell a client's Glaxo shares; stockbrokers Kerr and Allen confirmed signatures and Glaxo registered the transfers.
Glaxo recovered from the stockbrokers, who sought contribution from Gordon's co-partners McHugh and Lynch.
The partners sought to amend their defence to deny vicarious liability and allege the stockbrokers' negligence broke the chain of causation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court against summary judgment for the stockbrokers on partnership liability.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no real prospect of showing Gordon's fraud was outside the ordinary course of the firm's business or that stockbrokers' negligence broke causation.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 10 of the Partnership Act 1890, applying Dubai Aluminium's close-connection test, a partner's fraudulent share dealings may be in the ordinary course of an accountancy firm's business where the firm occasionally handled share transactions; fraud is the sole cause of loss and a third party's failure to detect forgery does not break the chain.
legal_issues: Whether Gordon's forged share transfers were done in the ordinary course of the firm's business
Application of the close-connection test from Dubai Aluminium Co Ltd v Salaam
Whether stockbrokers' negligent signature confirmation broke the chain of causation
Whether contribution was available under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978

enrichment.short_title: Rent review counter-notice invalid where tenant's solicitor knew landlord's changed address but tenant did not serve there
key_facts: Arundel served a rent review notice increasing annual rent to £30,000; Khokher disputed service of a valid counter-notice.

The Court of Appeal held valid service required the last known place of business, which the tenant's solicitor knew had moved to Wheathampstead.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Resumed appeal to the Court of Appeal after permission to adduce fresh evidence on rent review service and sub-letting consent.

enrichment.short_title: Unique employee may have normal retiring age equal to contractual retirement age under ERA s109(1)(a)(i)
key_facts: Wall was Director-General of BCAS with an agreed contractual retirement age of 70 but was dismissed at 67.
The employment tribunal and EAT proceeded on agreed assumptions that his position was unique and his contractual retiring age was 70.
The EAT held a normal retiring age of 70 existed; BCAS appealed, relying on Age Concern Scotland v Hines.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on a preliminary jurisdictional point under section 109.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority (Simon Brown LJ and Scott Baker LJ; Evans-Lombe J dissenting); complaint remitted to the employment tribunal on merits.
enrichment.ratio: The word 'normal' in section 109(1)(a)(i) does not require comparators; an employee in a unique position with a contractual retiring age may have that age as his normal retiring age, determined by what age he could reasonably expect to be compelled to retire.

enrichment.short_title: HSE decision not to prosecute landlords after child's death by falling door held not unlawful

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999

key_facts: Christopher Pullen, aged 12, was killed when a heavy communal security door fell on him at Southdown House on Islington's Market Estate.
Islington owned the estate; Hyde Housing Association held the maintenance contract from July 2000.
The HSE investigated but decided there was no realistic prospect of convicting either body under section 3.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the Health and Safety Executive's decision not to prosecute Islington and Hyde.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; HSE decision held reasonably open on the evidence and correctly applying the Code for Crown Prosecutors.
enrichment.ratio: A decision not to prosecute is reviewable only on narrow grounds including unlawful policy, failure to follow the Code, mistake of law, or perversity; where employers had reasonably practicable repair systems and evidence did not sufficiently establish how long the door had been dangerous or employee default, the HSE could reasonably conclude there was no realistic prospect of conviction.

Elements of section 3(1) HSWA and reverse burden under section 40

key_facts: Neighbours Tromans objected to detailed planning permission for a detached dwelling at 22 Washbrook Lane adjacent to their home.

enrichment.ratio: Where officers change recommendation after deferral, site visit, and satisfactory additional information on tree protection and retaining walls, a local planning authority is not required to give separate reasons in the committee minutes if the officer report adequately explains departure from earlier refusal grounds; alleged vote miscount by objectors does not render the process unfair where the chair verified the count.
